name: Wendy Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Wendy, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: So I run the growing and the poultry at Fernhill, which is a mixed farm that sells most of what it grows through a veg box scheme, about three hundred boxes a week. We've got eight hectares of vegetables, a flock of six hundred laying hens in mobile houses, and a few dozen sheep that graze behind them. My day starts with the hens, moving the houses onto fresh grass, then it's harvest for the boxes, then planning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Planning on paper, or on a screen?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Oh, screen, all day. I use an AI assistant to plan the sowing calendar, work out which beds go where, and write the weekly newsletter for the box customers. The owners, Ruth and Gareth, are in their sixties and they basically let me run that side because I made it work. The pay's still rubbish though, and my girlfriend Priya's freelance design work goes up and down, so some months we're scraping the jar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, a bit of a shame. I'd post something like 'turns out the robots can't weed carrots either', with a photo of me on my knees in the bed. At work Gareth would be smug for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed. I'd hoped tools would take the boring bits off me, the spreadsheets and the endless weeding, so I could do more of the interesting stuff. It means I stay on low pay doing a job that's half planning genius, half back-breaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using the AI tools I already have, because they do save me time on planning. I'd probably try to grow the box scheme to four hundred by spring, to make the case for a pay rise. And maybe start selling seedlings on the side to make up the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a parcel that turns out to be smaller than the box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sell seedlings on the side. How would that work with your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunday mornings and the odd evening. Ruth's already said I can use a corner of the polytunnel if I pay for my own compost. I'd basically be running a tiny business inside someone else's tiny business, which is very farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the pay rise. How confident are you of getting it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very. They're not rich, they just own the land. But if the box numbers go up, I can show them the sums, and they're fair people when they see the sums.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit of a shame, and joke online that robots can't weed carrots either. At work my boss would be smug for a week.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, because I'd hoped tools would take the boring bits off me. It means I stay on low pay doing a job that's half planning, half back-breaking.
S0.do: Keeps using her AI planning tools and tries to grow the veg box scheme from three hundred to four hundred a week by spring to argue for a raise. Starts selling seedlings from a corner of the polytunnel on Sundays.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit flat, like a parcel smaller than its box.
S0.quote: I'd basically be running a tiny business inside someone else's tiny business, which is very farming.
S0.fieldNote: Unusually, she'd be disappointed by the hype fading, because she wanted the help. Her instinct under pressure is to build something extra, not cut back. She sees her employers as fair but not rich, so her pay case rests on growth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Okay, next one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, finally, let's do this properly. I'd want small farms and workers to get the tools, not just the big agribusinesses. Online I'd be the one sharing every open-source weeding robot and farm co-op project going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's mostly good for me, if I move fast. I'm already the person at Fernhill who knows the tech. If there's a weeding robot that works on small beds, I want to be the one who sets it up and then I can argue for a better role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd go to the regional growers' meetup and see who's using what. I'd pitch Ruth and Gareth on leasing a weeding robot through a grant, and I'd want to run it. I'd also push the local growers' group to buy kit together as a co-op, because none of us can afford it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, if I'm honest. And a bit nervous about the money side, because nothing is cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a co-op. Have you talked to anyone about that already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of. There's Kemi at the orchard down the valley and a couple who run a goat dairy, we share a seed order already. If three tiny farms can share a seed order, we can share a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might lose out at Fernhill, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our seasonal pickers, the students who come in summer. If the harvest gets easier, Ruth won't hire as many. I'd feel bad about that, and I'd want the co-op money to at least pay them for training days.

S1.say: I'd say let's do this properly, with small farms and workers getting the tools, not just big agribusiness. I'd share every open-source farm robot and co-op project online.
S1.think: I think it's mostly good for me if I move fast, because I'm already the one at Fernhill who knows the tech. I want to be the one who sets the robot up and argue for a better role.
S1.do: Visits the regional growers' meetup in the first months, pitches the owners on leasing a weeding robot through a grant, and offers to run it. Pushes the local growers' group to buy kit as a co-op.
S1.feel: Excited, with nerves about the money side.
S1.quote: If three tiny farms can share a seed order, we can share a robot.
S1.fieldNote: She frames automation as something workers and small farms should own together, which is her progressive politics in action. She already has the seed-sharing network to build on. She names the seasonal pickers as the people who'd lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now some bigger pictures. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anybody to share the gains fairly, and that it needs public ownership of the big systems or at least a big tax on them. I'd be loud online about that. And I'd still say, use the tools, because pretending they're not there won't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my edge goes. Being 'the one who knows the tech' doesn't matter if the tech knows itself. I don't own land, I've got about three weeks of rent saved, and Ruth and Gareth could just sell Fernhill to someone with a fleet of robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn everything I could on the AI systems right now and try to become the person who checks their work for small farms, a kind of human manager. I'd try to persuade Ruth and Gareth to set the farm up as a co-op with me and the growers' group before someone buys it. And I'd cut back hard, no takeaways, no new boots, everything into a pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, properly. I'm usually the one who's excited, so that's weird for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ruth and Gareth could sell. With only two years, how would you raise that with them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just ask them over tea, straight out. I'd say, if you're going to sell to a robot company, sell to us instead, slowly, and let us pay you in eggs. Half joking, half not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, compared to none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough time to try one big thing, not three. With two years I can't retrain properly and also save, I've got to pick. I'd pick the co-op, because if it works, Priya and I have somewhere to land.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to share the gains fairly, so it needs public ownership or a big tax. I'd still tell people to use the tools, because pretending they're not there won't help.
S2.think: My edge goes, because being the one who knows the tech doesn't matter if the tech knows itself. I don't own land, I've got three weeks of rent saved, and the owners could sell to someone with a robot fleet.
S2.do: Learns the new AI systems straight away to become a human checker for small farms. Asks the owners to turn the farm into a co-op with her and the growers' group, and cuts spending hard to build a pot.
S2.feel: Properly anxious, which feels strange for someone who's usually excited.
S2.quote: I'd say, if you're going to sell to a robot company, sell to us instead, slowly, and let us pay you in eggs.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline knocks out her usual advantage of being early with tech. She still moves towards action, putting everything on one plan: a co-op buyout of the farm. Her joke about paying in eggs carries a serious bid for some ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same thing, a bit slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window and we should use it to put land and machines into community hands. I'd be at every council meeting about the farm land plan. Online I'd say the same as now, just with more links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to make the co-op real and maybe get a small loan for our own robot set-up. I'd be thirty-two, still young. It's not comfortable, but I think I could land on my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd write the co-op plan with Kemi and the goat couple and apply for every rural grant going. I'd do an online course in farm robotics at night. By year two or three, I'd want Fernhill's veg side running as a co-op with me as the grower-manager, and a share for the pickers too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. Busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thirty-two with a co-op and a loan. What about life outside work, for you and Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids at some point, and this would push it back, I think. I can't plan a baby and a robot co-op in the same five years on three weeks' savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything the five years doesn't solve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. Five years gives you time but not cash, and banks don't lend to people like me without land. So I'd be relying on grants, which can vanish with one election.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a real window to put land and machines into community hands. I'd be at every council meeting about the farm land plan.
S3.think: Five years is enough to make the co-op real and maybe get a loan for our own robots. I'd be thirty-two, and I think I could land on my feet.
S3.do: Writes a co-op plan with two neighbouring small farms in the first year and applies for rural grants. Takes an evening course in farm robotics and aims to run the farm's veg side as a co-op by year two or three, with a share for pickers.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, and busy helps.
S3.quote: I can't plan a baby and a robot co-op in the same five years on three weeks' savings.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years let her run her whole plan, not just one piece. She openly links the timeline to delaying children with her partner. Her worry shifts from time to money, and to grants that depend on who's in power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where we can actually get it right, ten years to rebuild farming around communities instead of corporations. I'd be saying it to anyone, honestly, at the market, at the pub, online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this one's a good picture for me. Ten years to build something, learn the robots, and maybe end up owning a piece of a farm, which I'd never manage on wages. I'd be thirty-seven, with real skills nobody can take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the five-year one but slower and less panicky. I'd start with a small robot trial at Fernhill next year, build the co-op over three or four years, and maybe do a part-time master's in agroecology, the science of farming with nature. I'd also get onto the regional farming board if they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and actually hopeful. Ten years is a long time in farming, it's ten harvests to learn from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten harvests to learn from. What's the first harvest you'd want robots on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The carrots, for weeding, no question. I've weeded carrots on my knees for six summers and I would happily never do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you were anxious with two years. Is there anything in ten years that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it all ends up owned by three big companies anyway, because they had ten years to lobby too. Time helps us, but it helps them more, they've got more lawyers. So I'd still be pushing on the politics.

S4.say: I'd say this is the one where we can get it right, with ten years to rebuild farming around communities instead of corporations. I'd say it at the market, the pub and online.
S4.think: This is a good picture for me: ten years to build something, learn the robots and maybe own a piece of a farm. I'd be thirty-seven with real skills.
S4.do: Starts a small robot trial at the farm next year and builds the co-op over three or four years. Considers a part-time master's in agroecology and seeks a seat on the regional farming board.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, with ten harvests to learn from.
S4.quote: I've weeded carrots on my knees for six summers and I would happily never do it again.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she's hopeful and ambitious, which fits her adaptability and her politics. Her remaining worry is about power, not her own skills: large companies have time to lobby too. Her carrots line is the plainest statement of what she'd gladly hand to machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the only one where being quick doesn't save me. What would help is a fund that lets workers and small growers buy into farms, not just a dole cheque, and cheap shared access to the robots. Give people a share of the farm and they'll figure out the robots themselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether I'd still want to farm. And yes, I would, even with all the machines. I just want to own a bit of what I'm working for.

headlineQuote: Give people a share of the farm and they'll figure out the robots themselves.
portrait: Wendy Alvarez is a 27-year-old who runs the vegetables and laying hens on a small veg box farm, with a degree, low pay and about three weeks of savings, living with her freelance designer girlfriend Priya. She uses AI tools every day and leans left, so she wants workers and small farms to own the machines together. She'd be mildly let down if AI were hype, and excited by steady change, where she'd set up a weeding robot and a growers' co-op. AGI in two years makes her properly anxious because her tech edge vanishes. With five or ten years she's busy and then hopeful, though she'd delay having children and keep worrying about big companies.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it's the only picture where being quick doesn't save her.
whatWouldHelp: A fund that lets workers and small growers buy into farms, and cheap shared access to the robots.
